items.title: ECG trains 23 Ashanti engineers to detect equipment faults before outages
items.description: Twenty-three technicians and engineers of the Ashanti Sub-Transmission Region of the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) have received training in infrared thermography to strengthen preventive maintenance and reduce equipment-related outages. ‎‎The 2-day intensive training in Kumasi is to equip sub-transmission technical staff with skills to detect abnormal heat, commonly referred to as “hotspots,” on critical electrical infrastructure before it develops into major faults. For over 10 years, ECG has been using infrared thermography, which uses thermal imaging cameras to identify unusual temperature patterns on substations, pylons, cables, switchgear, and other equipment. This enables maintenance teams to intervene before failure occurs. It saw beneficiaries selected from the various sub-transmission technical sections, such as protection and control, network maintenance, substation and switchgear maintenance, as well as control operations, receiving face-to-face tutorials from experienced facilitators. ‎‎The programme, which combined classroom theory with practical field exercises, was opened by the Acting General Manager of Ashanti Sub-Transmission, Ing. Christopher Anafo, with Ing. Randy Delanyo Adjorlolo from the headquarters of ECG as facilitator. ‎‎“This training is a proactive step towards strengthening ECG’s preventive maintenance culture,” Ing. Adjorlolo said. Participants try their hands on infrared thermography during a field exercise ‎‎Ing. Edem Evans Agra, Substation and Switchgear Maintenance Manager, said the technology will help the region take early corrective action. ‎‎“Early detection of hotspots will reduce unexpected equipment failures, minimise power interruptions, and extend the lifespan of critical assets. It is about protecting our network and serving customers better,” he said. The ‎Head of Public Relations for Ashanti Sub-Transmission, Collins Manu, who later briefed the media on the exercise, said the initiative complements ECG’s ongoing network improvement efforts. ‎‎“While the company invests in network upgrades, Ashanti Sub-Transmission is also working proactively to identify and mitigate potential faults before they affect customers,” he said. ‎‎The training forms part of ECG’s broader strategy to enhance operational efficiency and improve reliability of electricity supply across the Ashanti Region.

items.title: Party in the (Downwardly Mobile) U.S.A.
items.description: With every passing year, Miley Cyrus’s 2009 single “Party in the U.S.A.” comes to feel more like an artifact of an empire before its fall. When the Disney Channel star sang about hopping off the plane at LAX with a dream and a cardigan—on the way to turn her country-girl ambitions of fame into Hollywood reality—she projected an image of a nation that still believed in its own myths, trusted its power centers, and grooved together to the same songs. The guitars fizzed like a fresh can of Coke, and Cyrus advertised to the world’s strivers that making it in America is a breeze. Released less than a year after the 2008 financial crash, “Party in the U.S.A.” was part of a crop of songs that have, in recent years, been labeled “recession pop.” It’s an affectionate term for happy, uncomplicated anthems—think Katy Perry’s “Teenage Dream” or the Black Eyed Peas’ “I Gotta Feeling”—that once distracted from headlines about bailouts and foreclosures. The optimism of those songs now seems rarer in American life, but over the past few years, TikTok pundits and media commentators have theorized that a new wave of recession pop might come “back” to suit the economic weirdness of the mid-2020s. [ Read: Is this the worst-ever era of American pop culture? ] I’ve never really bought that argument, for a few reasons. Perky pop largely faded from the charts in the mid-2010s not because of the national mood but because of changes in how people listen: Streaming eroded the top-down distribution channels, such as radio and network TV, that loved to broadcast sugary, universally appealing sing-alongs. More audience-segmented styles—country, hip-hop, confessional bedroom songwriters—now rule the charts. So-called pure pop has become a subculture , almost akin to indie rock. And what’s been happening lately in that subculture is more interesting than a mere revival of carefree times. This summer has served up a slate of great party songs that are full of twisted nostalgia and tarnished glamour. Pop is dancing in the ruins of the American dream—or at least in the ruins of the traditional record business. “Party in the U.S.A.” came to mind while I was listening to “ Ain’t in LA ,” a tasty new single by the rising star Adéla. She is a 22-year-old Slovakian musician who learned English by watching Hannah Montana , and the song is an obvious Cyrus homage. It revisits the trap-pop sound of Cyrus’s 2013 hit “We Can’t Stop” and features that song’s deep-voiced rapper, Theron Thomas. The breezy, yelled chorus seems designed to, as Cyrus put it in ’09, make the butterflies fly away. But the track has a naggingly wistful undercurrent—and its lyrics flip “Party in the U.S.A.” on its head. The verses describe the yearnings of a young girl with Madonna and Destiny’s Child posters pinned to her wall. She wants to be a star—but watching American media taught her that “her dreams don’t live at home.” Then the chorus booms a corrective: “It’s all a lie / The baddest bitches ain’t in LA.” In the music video, Adéla balls out in stereotypical ways—twerking, joyriding, writhing on top of a pile of gold trophies—in her hometown of Bratislava, alongside kid dancers in Slovakian folk garb. She has a message for “girls in them unknown cities”: It’s hot to stay put. Adéla would know. As a teenager, she traveled to Hollywood in hope of a big break on the 2023 reality show The Debut: Dream Academy . A co-production of Geffen Records and the Korean firm Hybe, the series recruited young women from around the world to audition to be part of a girl group subjected to the rigorous management style of K-pop. A trained ballerina with a fierce pout, Adéla performed strongly—but after she was criticized for not perfectly gelling with the other performers, she became one of the first girls cut from the running. Dream Academy represented the response of the U.S.’s faltering star-making machine to international competition. Over the past decade or so, K-pop has become the premiere global source of the sort of polished dance-pop that homegrown stars such as Beyoncé and Backstreet Boys once specialized in. Dream Academy sought to repurpose the K-pop model for performers who sing mostly in English and come from all over. The resulting band, the sextet Katseye, has put out a string of hyperactive, utterly frivolous songs —full of L.A. references to $20 smoothies and trysts in Bel Air—that have performed decently on the U.S. charts. But the continuing viability of this carefully stage-managed project is an open question: Two Katseye members are on hiatus for health-related reasons. Adéla, meanwhile, has embarked on a solo career that’s made her the connoisseur’s choice for girlish bangers. Although “Ain’t in LA” sounds clean and sleek, her earlier singles were a bit edgier, pairing dark electronica elements with lyrics about surviving the record industry’s manipulations. Her penchant for minor chords and meta-commentary recalls early Lady Gaga, but whereas that star subsumed her personal identity into operatic symbolism, Adéla’s music remains human-scale—bruised by rejection and panting with yearning. “Staring at a TV screen ’til I got bloody eyes / Just a little European girl, was plotting on my rise,” she squeals in “KGB,” sounding like someone whose childhood dreams have begun to smolder into a hunger for vengeance. An even grimier sense of desperation powers the most astonishing pop song of the year: “BEAT UP CHANEL$,” by the 29-year-old singer-songwriter Slayyyter. On paper, it could be part of the Broadway tradition of “I want” songs — this one sung by a character who covets MTV-typical treasures such as money, drugs, and handbags. But Hamilton this isn’t: Amid a clanging guitar and bass, Slayyyter screeches those desires like a caged fox. The track cycles between wild accelerations and gliding comedowns, gaining tornadic intensity. When a cheerful melody pops up at the end of the song, the effect is as life-affirming as stepping onto the platform after a terrifying roller-coaster ride. “I want something for real,” goes the final refrain. This gonzo song represents a culminating statement for an artist who’s been hustling for years. In the late 2010s, Slayyyter began to attract online attention for putting a deconstructed, sinister spin on Y2K pop. When I interviewed her in 2021 , she told me about being a teen girl in suburban St. Louis who was radicalized by the media’s harsh treatment of Britney Spears and Paris Hilton. Chasing stardom in the early 2020s, she moved to L.A. and recorded two dance-pop albums, themed around the horrors of fame, that pleased fans but received little attention more broadly. She’s said that she went into the studio for her third studio album, this year’s WOR$ST GIRL IN AMERICA , with the assumption that it would be her last. She thus let herself indulge extreme impulses: scuzzy production inspired by obscure artists from her old iPod, feral lyrics delivered in what she’s called a “tweaker twang” tone of voice. Many tracks seem to be about her own failure as a celebrity—“I’M ACTUALLY KINDA FAMOUS” is a glorious parody of the D-list mindset—and the album’s music videos have shown her back in her native Missouri, partying in tattered jeans among trailer parks. But though the album documents a breakdown, it has turned out to be her breakthrough. Released in March, WOR$ST GIRL IN AMERICA debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Dance Albums chart, drew her some big festival audiences, and earned her the fandom of Courtney Love . The buzz seems to still be growing: This month, Slayyyter scored her first-ever entry on the Hot 100. The track to achieve that feat is a sister song to “BEAT UP CHANEL$,” titled “brand new chanel$.” It’s entirely different from its predecessor but nearly as good: a blurry reimagining of the crisp, uplifting pulse of circa-2010 electronic dance music and pop punk. As with “Ain’t in LA,” a surprising amount of vulnerability lies beneath the song’s spiky attitude. Slayyyter sounds heartbroken about a cheating ex whose new woman, she sighs, wants brand-new Chanels—a villainous desire in a cultural moment when destroyed seems better than new. The urge to defy a mainstream that’s corrupted and fake has long been, of course, one of music history’s great drivers of progress. In trying to contextualize the sound that Slayyyter and her internet-pop peers in the share , Pitchfork just coined the fun term hyperclash . The name suggests a hybrid of the subgenres hyperpop (2010s laptoppers, many of them queer, subverting formulaic catchiness with video-game-inspired chaos) and electroclash (a late-’90s and early-2000s scene of ironic techno with punk influences). The writer Anna Gaca theorizes that hyperclash artists are drawn to hedonistic noise “as a protective adaptation amid the endless horrorscroll.” But if a trend is unfolding, it also involves pop musicians reckoning with the death of pop itself. Just as fans have lately become obsessed with the concept of the “flop,” artists are treating the archetype of the world-conquering superstar as an unattainable myth from a not-so-distant past. Singers who once projected glitz are having a blast with the aesthetics of downward mobility. [ Read: How Lizzo became one of pop culture’s great flops ] The acclaimed but under-the-radar singer Tinashe, for example, is promoting an album called Popstar . Her latest single is a trippy house song, “Melatonin,” that accuses people of “sleeping on” her—ignoring her greatness—and whose video is set in what looks like a foreclosed mansion. (In another single, the slinkily paranoid “Crash Out,” she sings, “The American dream is outdated.”) An equally telling example: Kim Petras, a 33-year-old German who’s spent years making bright and bland pop with the notorious producer Dr. Luke , recently went independent and put out her most experimental—and best—album yet, Detour . Her persona used to be that of a Malibu socialite. Now, on the swooning “Jeep,” she fantasizes about driving around gas-station parking lots, drinking Four Loko, and doing “middle-American shit.” None of these artists is rejecting the race for riches; we aren’t back in 2013, when Lorde mocked the “Cristal, Maybach, diamonds on your timepiece” she heard about on the radio. Rather, the mood is one of thwarted materialism, of wanting but not getting. And no one should mistake much of this wave for a meaningful rebellion against the industry. Adéla works with Capitol Records; Slayyyter joined Columbia Records to put out WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA . At a time when even the biggest stars seem a little niche , major-label backing doesn’t quite mean what it once did—but clearly, music’s power brokers have judged that a scuffed-up, striving sound might appeal to the public right now. It’s not difficult to see why. After a long pop-cultural swing away from Millennial do-goodery toward a redux of 1980s “greed is good” aesthetics, burnout with chasing the bag is finally setting in. Many influencers are starting to see their reach wane ; luxury brands are facing flatlining sales . At the same time, anti-institutionalist sentiment—whether directed at political parties, Big Tech, or the entertainment business—is at a high. “Party in the U.S.A.” landed at a time when people still regarded Hollywood as a land of magic, not as a playground for sex traffickers. The most popular songs of late reflects these trends as well. Ella Langley’s record-setting charts run with “Choosin’ Texas” speaks to a demand for music that’s indifferent to the cosmopolitan hustle. The stateside appeal of non-English-language stars also represents shifting ideals of what success looks and sounds like. Just as Adéla advises that the baddest bitches ain’t in L.A., Bad Bunny scoffs at the idea that Puerto Ricans need to head to the mainland United States to make their dreams come true. In these conditions, it’s no wonder that pop, once the sound of the center, is finding glamour in marginality. Stars who might otherwise aspire to godhood are meeting listeners where they’ve always been: partying in their own backyard, with their own friends, and on their own terms—even while dreaming of something bigger.

items.title: Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
items.description: Last Tuesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei hosted a wake for his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Among the thousands who thronged Tehran’s biggest mosque were the country’s most prominent political figures and several of the elder Khamenei’s sons. One person was notably absent: Mojtaba, the event’s official host. Almost six months since his anointment, Iran’s supreme leader has been entirely obscured from the public eye. Not a single contemporaneous picture, video, or audio recording of him has been released. Many of the country’s top political leaders admit that they haven’t seen him—among them Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister and a member of the National Security Council. IranWire , a London-based opposition outlet, reports that not a single cabinet member has met with Mojtaba since he became supreme leader. Not even Mojtaba’s close friends and relatives have seen him. Fewer than five people have met with Mojtaba since his ascent to power, Mohammad Hossein Khoshvaght, a former official and a relative of Mojataba’s told me, “due to security precautions.” The rationale is not implausible. Mojtaba would be a likely target for an Israeli or U.S. air strike, such as the one that killed his father. Direct communication from him could supply Iran’s enemies with clues to his whereabouts. He is also said to have sustained injuries in the February strike on his family that have made public speeches and appearances difficult. [ Graeme Wood: ‘The most dangerous man in the world’ ] But the totality of Mojtaba’s invisibility and a recent decline in statements from his office have set Tehran abuzz with new rumors of his death. Some sources inside and close to the government speculated to me that Mojtaba recently died from the injuries that he had sustained in February. And irrespective of his actual status, the uncertainty might have major implications for Iran. “I believe Mojtaba has either passed away or is brain-dead,” a staffer at a government institution in Tehran told me, citing the tailing off of even indirect communication from the leader to the outside world. At least two other government officials told me the same. One said that he believed Mojtaba died or became brain-dead earlier this month. Two sources in the Iranian government recently told IranWire that word had spread among those at the “highest level of the regime” that Mojtaba was doing very poorly and could die at any moment. About two weeks ago, a public appeal went out on a domestic messaging service, asking Iranians to pray for Mojtaba’s health and sacrifice sheep to bless him, as is customary in Islam. Mojtaba’s life was “under threat,” and some “clerics” had warned that he might be killed, the appeal said. Since he was appointed, Mojtaba has ruled by decrees disseminated by his office. Iran’s supreme leader is a religious authority in addition to being the head of state, and on July 27, Mojtaba’s office published a list of his answers to practical questions posed by the devout. One correspondent had requested guidance on eating with bleeding gums, because blood is haram — forbidden—in Islam. Any food contaminated with blood, including from one’s own gums, must be thrown out, Mojtaba ruled. If his office is to be believed, then the leader was well enough to ponder Islamic law and issue relevant rulings as recently as a month ago. The office’s most recent statement came on August 9 and reported that Mojtaba had met with President Masoud Pezeshkian. It didn’t say when the meeting had taken place but noted that it was on the occasion of the president’s third year in office, which puts it on or after July 28. Pezeshkian confirmed to the Iranian media that he spent seven hours with Mojtaba discussing the war and the country’s beleaguered economy. (According to Khoshvaght, Pezeshkian was taken to that meeting “without knowing where it was,” which suggests that he was transported blindfolded, mafia-style.) Also on August 9, Mojtaba issued a slew of decrees, appointing several generals to top military positions and swapping out one of his representatives on the National Security Council. Since then, the office has been silent. Khoshvaght assured me that Mojtaba is definitely alive. The rumors about the leader’s death are “part of a psychological war hoping to demoralize Iran’s officials and its people, for them to give up to the pressures and threats of America,” he said. He added that the rumors also aim to embolden Iranians opposed to the regime, giving them “courage to come to the streets so that the plans of the U.S. and Israel can be realized.” Abdolreza Davari, a former adviser to the interior ministry and a vocal supporter of Mojtaba’s, told me that the leader is “in full health” and will soon be revealed to the public. But the two weeks with no communication, the public appeal for sheep sacrifice, and the rumors emanating from government circles have led many Iranians to doubt such assurances. Whether Mojtaba is dead or alive, his public absence creates problems for the Iranian regime. The supreme leader holds most of the constitutional power in the Islamic Republic and has in the past served as the final arbiter among the system’s warring factions and institutions. Mojtaba appears to be sitting these conflicts out, at a moment when their outcome could be particularly consequential. [ Robert Kagan: Iran unleashed ] The country’s 13-person National Security Council is effectively running the country as a collective. It is chaired by Pezeshkian, a reformist who favors an end to the war with America, and includes Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the powerful parliamentary speaker who led the talks with the United States. But it also includes General Ahmad Vahidi, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and other military leaders. Back in June, 12 of the council’s 13 members voted in favor of the memorandum of understanding that Iran reached with the United States in Islamabad. Mojtaba sent a message endorsing the deal but also noting that he had initially opposed such an agreement “in principle.” Hard-line critics of diplomacy seized on this to claim that Ghalibaf had usurped power and forced the memorandum on the leader. A news outlet linked to a faction in the IRGC even issued a documentary called Ghalibaf’s Coup . Mojtaba neither endorsed this view nor put it to rest. Rather, he has remained mum as various factions have purported to speak for him. Pezeshkian has told reporters that in his meeting with Mojtaba, the leader stressed that regime officials should “keep unity and cohesion” and avoid infighting. But the infighting goes on. In June, a statement signed by 63 of the 88 members of the Assembly of Experts, a clerical body tasked with supervising the supreme leader, admonished regime officials that none of them was authorized to act against Mojtaba’s “definite opinion.” At the same time, the statement called on any Muslim “who could gain access” to kill Donald Trump—not quite the message of Iran’s negotiators, but rather more consonant with Mojtaba’s statements promising “blood revenge.” The Iranian regime has existential choices to make as it decides between diplomacy and conflict. Iran’s constitution is clear about who has the authority to set the country’s course. But no one seems able to say for sure whether that person is alive or dead. And without a firm hand at the top, indecision can become a purgatory without a foreseeable end.

items.title: The Jews Who Voted for Hitler
items.description: On the evening of February 5, 1930, the art and theater critic Paul Fechter took the podium before the League of Nationalist German Jews, in Berlin, to discuss purported Jewish control of the press and the arts in the country. “When Dr. Max Naumann invited me to give a lecture in your circle, I rather impulsively said yes,” Fechter began. “When he then told me the topic he wanted me to address, my immediate reaction was: Good grief ! One could not have found a better topic for making oneself thoroughly unpopular and for antagonizing everyone in the room.” For too long, Fechter said, people had been too “shy, fearful, cautious” to speak openly about the Jews. Fechter, an editor at the conservative newspaper Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung , was pulling no punches. The popular Jewish humorist Kurt Tucholsky, Fechter said, had insulted the German people with his recent book, Deutschland, Deutschland über alles , an acid satire about the army, the police, the civil service, the national anthem, even Sekt , a popular sparkling wine. “A large portion of the literary and art worlds are in Jewish hands,” Fechter continued. “The theaters, the major publishing houses, the major art dealers are all at least partially under Jewish control.” Jewish art dealers, Fechter said, filled their galleries with works by “Manet and Monet and Renoir and Gauguin and Picasso and Cezanne”—French Impressionists and Modernists, in other words, rather than traditional German painters. The Antigermanismus among Jews, Fechter declared, was “far more robust” than the Antisemitismus among right-wing German nationalists. Naumann, the founder of the league, published the Fechter tirade in his monthly publication , The Nationalist German Jew , circulated to his group’s 7,000 members, mostly middle-class professionals in more than 20 chapters around the country. Naumann himself was a Berlin-based Jewish attorney who was decidedly antidemocratic, belligerently nationalistic, and unapologetically critical of other Jews. He blamed Ostjuden —the “Eastern Jews” fleeing pogroms in Russia, Romania, Austria, Hungary, Poland, and elsewhere—for flooding the country with unwanted immigrants. He felt pity but no solidarity. “It is the same pity we feel when there is talk of the Turks massacring Armenians or of lynch mobs targeting black people in America,” Naumann wrote—an abstract pity without emotional connection. In his league’s founding treatise, On Nationalist German Jews , published in 1920, Naumann had compared Zionists, those seeking a Jewish homeland in Palestine, to Nazis, whose political movement had just been founded. “Both groups, the fanatics of Zion and the knights of the swastika, are basically the same in that they have turned a question of ancestry into a question of nationality,” Naumann argued. Naumann defended his German and Jewish identities in equal measure, a stance reflected in the term nationaldeutscher Jude —a blood-and-soil German Jew. [ Timothy W. Ryback: How Hitler dismantled a democracy in 53 days ] Naumann drifted right with the rest of German politics in the early 1930s, first abiding and then supporting the extremist, right-wing, rabidly anti-Semitic positions of Adolf Hitler. It is impossible to imagine a more tragically misplaced political calculation than Naumann’s embrace of national socialism. Though the Hitler Juden —or Nazi Jews, as Naumann’s adherents came to be known—represented less than 2 percent of Germany’s half-million Jews, they provide a cautionary tale of members of a minority within a minority who cast their lot with a political leader who openly despised them. Naumann was born in 1875 into a middle-class family—bankers, landowners, cloth merchants—in an era of unprecedented opportunity for German Jews. They had recently gained the right to vote. They could run for office. They enjoyed equal protection under the law. Professions formerly restricted were now open—law, medicine, academia. Naumann studied jurisprudence at the Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin, where he joined a fraternity and was given a Schmiss across his chin, the honorific dueling scar of a true Prussian. But prejudice persisted. When Naumann was denied an officer’s title in the Prussian military because of his Jewish heritage, he enlisted in the 2nd Bavarian Infantry Regiment. Naumann advanced through the ranks, from lieutenant to first lieutenant and eventually to captain, serving with distinction during the First World War. He was awarded an Iron Cross First Class and an Iron Cross Second Class, among other decorations, for “outstandingly brave deeds performed in the face of the enemy that went far beyond the call of duty.” But Jewish veterans of the Great War returned to find Jews collectively vilified for Germany’s defeat and surrender. The Reich Federation of Jewish Front-Line Soldiers countered with an information campaign highlighting their commitment and sacrifice—100,000 Jewish soldiers had served at the front; 35,000 had been decorated for bravery; 12,000 had given their lives for the fatherland. The Central Association of German Citizens of Jewish Faith, or Centralverein, sought to combat rising anti-Semitism through legal protections of Jewish identity and heritage. Meanwhile, the Zionist Federation of Germany urged German Jews to immigrate to Palestine for their own safety. [ From the World War I issue: Reinhold Niebuhr on Hitler, reduced to impotence ] Naumann found these responses wholly inadequate or misguided. He denounced the members of the Centralverein as ineffective “ Dummköpfe ,” or idiots, and the Zionists as traitors, foremost among them “the world-famous scholar Einstein,” who placed his Jewish identity over his German heritage. “The spiritual and even the material misery of the Jews in Germany would never have assumed such frightening proportions,” Naumann claimed in 1927, “if steps had been taken in time to prevent the Zionists, and especially the Zionist Ostjuden , from positioning themselves before Jews and non-Jews alike as the only rightful spokesmen of Judaism.” Naumann believed that anti-Semitism needed to be “dismantled,” not legally challenged, the Centralverein’s preferred approach. During the war, Naumann had watched anti-Semitic sentiment evaporate in the heat of battle, where what mattered, he later recalled, were “actions,” not “words,” and where “a tough, resilient, determined willingness to put one’s head on the line” for comrades and the fatherland “transcended all class and racial difference.” This was the experience that shaped his approach to German politics. He was joined by Alfred Peyser, the chair of the League of Nationalist German Jews, who was also an eminent physician and the municipal counselor of an upscale Berlin district. In a foundational 1922 essay defining the concept of a “nationalist German” Jew, Peyser warned fellow Jewish Germans against returning to “ Ghettoknechtschaft ”—enslavement to the ghetto—or trying to escape to “Zion,” urging them instead to embrace the “German fatherland.” “Yes, we love this land, its language, its people,” Peyser wrote. “We feel as one with it!” Naumann and Peyser found a powerful ally in Samuel Breslauer, the editor of the Berliner Lokal-Anzeiger , a popular conservative newspaper. Breslauer traveled to New York City in the spring of 1927 with a delegation of German newspaper editors to meet with their American counterparts, including Adolph Ochs, the publisher of The New York Times . Breslauer advocated for fierce German nationalism and equally fervent Judaism. He defended this duality in an article titled “Me, an Antisemite.” “If over the course of three decades I have undergone a change,” Breslauer wrote, it had been a political drift to the right—but “certainly not” away from Judaism. Instead, he insisted, his Judaism had deepened and strengthened—“in the religious, not in the ethnic-national sense.” Naumann had initially aligned his league with the German People’s Party, a center-right party led by the Nobel laureate Gustav Stresemann. But the political picture changed in September 1930, when the National Socialists surged nearly tenfold in national elections. Fascism was suddenly fashionable. Siegfried “Fred” Bon, the Jewish author of a three-volume philosophical treatise, Does 2 x 2 = 4? , sought to square Judaism and national socialism. In a January 1931 article for The Nationalist German Jew , Bon cataloged Jewish contributors to the country’s conservative movements, foremost among them Walther Rathenau, a foreign minister in the Weimar Republic and the first person, according to Bon, who’d sought to merge nationalism with socialism—“the very positions that today constitute the foundations of the National Socialist program.” Bon’s article appeared under the title “Can Jews Be National Socialists?” Naumann, for his part, suggested that they could be, and he pointed to Italy as evidence. Jews had joined Benito Mussolini in the 1922 March on Rome. Guido Jung, a Jew, was Italy’s fascist minister of finance. Renzo Ravenna, a Jew, was the fascist mayor of Ferrara. When Girolamo Bassi, a Jewish lawyer in Venice, faced financial difficulties, a judge suggested that he join Mussolini’s Partito Nazionale Fascista. “So, two months later, my father became a cardcarrying Fascist,” Bassi’s son Roberto later recalled, “and having bought a fine black uniform went with the others to demonstrate support for Il Duce .” [ Timothy W. Ryback: The oligarchs who came to regret supporting Hitler ] Naumann attributed the fascist receptiveness toward Jews in Italy not only to the absence of Zionists and Ostjuden in that country but also to Jews’ absence from “intellectual” professions. Naumann urged young German Jews to pursue careers in trades such as carpentry and masonry rather than professions such as law and medicine. “Of the approximately 200,000 Jews in Italy, at most 10% are doctors, lawyers, and journalists,” The Nationalist German Jew reported in a 1933 article titled “Why There Is No Hatred of the Jews in Italy.” (Although it’s true that there was less anti-Semitism in Italy than in Germany, the article’s premise would be proved grimly wrong when Italy passed a series of discriminatory racial laws starting in 1938 and deported Jews to Nazi extermination camps.) In July 1932, Naumann caused a sensation when he appeared to urge German Jews to vote National Socialist in the upcoming Reichstag elections. In an article in Fechter’s newspaper, Naumann claimed that national socialism was the only viable future for the country—“that here, and only here, a path is being forged that can lead to a rebirth of Germanness and to the restoration of German prestige.” Centralverein was outraged. An op-ed in the organization’s newspaper, Central-Verein-Zeitung , lambasted Naumann for inaccuracy and irresponsibility, and argued that to discount the threat posed by Nazi anti-Semitism was absurdly credulous. Whatever common values Naumann shared with Hitler—anti-communist, antirepublican, antidemocratic—hatred of Jews remained foundational to Nazi ideology. Central-Verein-Zeitung reminded Naumann of the Nazis’ “unbridled attacks” and “public incitement” against Jews, noting that “Herr Hitler has never, on any occasion, contradicted the speakers of his own party regarding their stance on the Jewish question.” But Naumann continued to believe that the heated rhetoric against the Jews was political posturing that would cool once Hitler was in office, and once the inciting political effects of Jewish Communists, socialists, and Zionists had been neutralized. A trove of about 11 million digitized National Socialist records, analyzed by an international group of scholars from Harvard and elsewhere in a National Bureau of Economic Research paper published last April, includes 580 personal statements by Nazis, given in 1934, explaining their reasons for joining the party. Fully 26 percent of these Nazis cited their dislike of Jews as an “explicit causal reason” for joining the party, which suggests that anti-Semitism was considerably more than an incidental element of the party’s ideology. But Naumann was fixated on the other motivations for joining the party, which are reflected in the scholars’ analysis of these statements: 63 percent cited a hope for national renewal and the restoration of public order, while 53 percent expressed a desire for social belonging, 49 percent the need to combat communism, and 29 percent the belief that the party could lift them out of economic hardship. Naumann’s fatally naive view was that if these other concerns could be addressed, anti-Semitism would be diminished. Following Hitler’s appointment as chancellor, in January 1933, anti-Semitic violence spiked horrifically. Jews were assaulted on the street, at their places of business, in their homes. One young man was lashed bloody, then had pepper rubbed in his wounds to heighten the agony; he died of sepsis. An apartment on Berlin’s fashionable Friedrichstrasse was repurposed as a torture room, its walls spattered with blood. The foreign press chronicled the atrocities prominently. On March 25, Hermann Göring, the powerful Nazi cabinet minister, summoned Naumann and other Jewish leaders to his office. Göring read from a stack of foreign-newspaper clippings with growing fury. “Unless you put a stop to these libelous accusations immediately,” Göring said, “I shall no longer be able to vouch for the safety of the German Jews!” Naumann had intended to use the meeting to protest the rising anti-Semitic violence; to that end, he confronted Göring with a list of attacks on Jews. But he left the meeting as a propagandist for the Third Reich. “While we readily acknowledge that there are excesses against German Jews,” Naumann declared in a public statement, “we are not interested in foreign interference in our internal affairs.” To his fellow Jews of German heritage, Naumann counseled patience. “Today we are enduring without question days of rage,” he wrote in May. “It was inevitable that this anger—built up and heightened over fourteen years—would initially erupt in an explosive outburst.” But Naumann anticipated the day, “in the not too distant future,” when the country’s anti-Semitic fever would break and “Aryan and Jew” would once again “join hands” in common cause for the fatherland. “When this day of self-reflection finally arrives,” Naumann wrote, “that will be the beginning of the real answer to the German Jewish question.” The preceding month, however, Hitler’s government had enacted the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, which banned “non-Aryans” from government posts, as well as the Law on Admission to the Legal Profession, which prevented Jews—including Naumann—from practicing law. The Law Against Overcrowding in German Schools and Universities, passed at the same time, restricted the enrollment of Jewish students. Amid these draconian measures, Hans Heinrich Peyser, the son of Alfred Peyser, ran into Naumann one day on the Berlin subway. Naumann was just returning from a meeting with leaders of the Nazi storm troopers. He spoke to Peyser of the Nazis’ “high ideals” and the need to try to understand things from their perspective. “I found this excessive self-absorption and inward-looking preoccupation, in light of what had already happened in Germany, to be absolutely grotesque,” Peyser wrote. [ From the April 1932 issue: Hitler and Hitlerism: Germany under the Nazis ] The Jewish Telegraphic Agency, in New York, a wire service covering the global Jewish community, viewed Naumann and his adherents with similar dismay. “Although their professions have been taken away from them, and although they live in a state of rigid suspense and fear of the moment when they will be humiliated, beaten, or imprisoned, a large number of German Jews continue to remain faithful to the fatherland,” the agency reported on August 13. The report noted Naumann’s denunciation of Zionists as “traitors to their country.” Stories circulated of “Naumann Jews” ending their meetings with Hitler salutes and the singing of “ Horst Wessel Lied ,” the Nazi Party anthem. Though Naumann dismissed the alleged singing as “Jewish horror stories,” he defended the stiff-armed salutes and the presence of Nazi banners, saying that Jews needed to “overcome their fear of the swastika”: “After all, the Christian cross,” he wrote in April 1934, is also a symbol “in opposition to Judaism,” but “for a long time now no reasonable Jew has refused to accept the Iron Cross or other cross-shaped decoration.” In August of that year, when Reich President Paul von Hindenburg died, Naumann urged Jews to approve a public referendum transferring Hindenburg’s powers to Hitler in his capacity as chancellor, effectively handing Hitler unchallenged dictatorial rule. (He did so despite acknowledging to his fellow Jews that the Nazi regime had “brought rigors to us.”) “We urge all Jews who feel themselves Germans to vote ‘Yes’ on Aug. 19,” Naumann declared. Naumann reaffirmed his solidarity with Hitler’s government the following week, when he dispatched a telegram to the Nazi leader informing him that the League of Nationalist German Jews would not be attending a conference in Geneva for the establishment of the World Jewish Congress. Learning of this, Pariser Tageblatt , a newspaper for anti-Nazis in exile, responded: “Thank God!” A Gestapo report on a meeting of 400 nationalist German Jews in Berlin on May 27, 1935, confirms that Naumann’s support for Hitler persisted. Naumann “emphasized in particular that the members considered themselves genuine Germans,” the report noted, and “had welcomed the transformation in Germany brought about by the Führer.” The meeting ended with a rousing chorus of “ Deutschland, Deutschland über alles .” For all Naumann’s efforts to win approval or recognition from Nazi leaders for his organization, or for his view on what Jews’ place in the Third Reich should be, he never received any. On September 15, 1935, Hitler’s government introduced the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor, collectively known as the Nuremberg Laws, stripping Naumann and half a million other Jewish Germans of their citizenship. By then, Naumann was divorced, and his daughter had broken irreparably with him over his pro-Nazi position. On November 18, Naumann’s league was forcibly disbanded. Naumann himself was arrested by the Gestapo that same day and taken to Columbia-Haus, an SS detention and torture facility. A few weeks later, after attempting to commit suicide by slitting his wrists with the glass from his spectacles, Naumann was released. He died of cancer in May 1939, isolated and abandoned. By that point, thousands of Jews had escaped abroad. Alfred Peyser was stripped of his medical license and briefly incarcerated before immigrating to Sweden in 1939, where he survived the war. Other Naumann Jews were not so fortunate. Siegfried “Fred” Bon was dispatched to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in September 1940; he was executed there in April 1944. Samuel Breslauer, who lost his editorial post and his property to the Nazis, also perished in Theresienstadt, along with his wife, Bertha. Naumann’s remains were interred in a Protestant cemetery in the town of Stahnsdorf, southwest of Berlin, where his headstone still stands. It bears his name and military rank, along with his dates of birth and death, but no indication of faith or family. Persecuted and forgotten as a Jew, he was buried as he’d wished to be—as a German. This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “The Jews Who Voted for Hitler.”

items.title: Mahama calls for stronger health regulation to protect patients across Africa
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called on African countries to strengthen health regulation and collaboration to protect patients and boost public confidence in healthcare systems. Speaking at the 28th Annual International Conference of the Association of Medical Councils of Africa in Accra, President Mahama said achieving universal health coverage should not be limited to providing access to healthcare but must also ensure safety, quality, ethical standards, and accountability. He identified several emerging challenges facing healthcare systems, including the rapid expansion of digital health and artificial intelligence, the migration of health professionals, forged qualifications, humanitarian crises and the increasing spread of misinformation. President Mahama called on health regulators across Africa to improve cross-border cooperation, strengthen the verification of professional credentials, protect health data, and establish suitable frameworks for regulating digital health and artificial intelligence. He stressed that AI should complement professional judgement and human responsibility rather than replace them. Touching on Ghana’s health agenda, the president said the National Health Insurance Scheme currently covers about 76 percent of the population, with the government aiming to increase coverage to 90 percent. He also pointed to the rollout of the Free Primary Healthcare Programme in about 160 districts and efforts to expand local pharmaceutical production. President Mahama urged African countries to work together to develop health systems that are African-owned, meet global standards, and remain firmly focused on protecting the public. He subsequently declared the 28th Annual International Conference of the Association of Medical Councils of Africa officially open.

items.title: Ghana’s rent prices remain high despite lower inflation – TUC official
items.description: Deputy General Secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), Dr Kwabena Nyarko Otoo, has said Ghana’s rent prices remain high despite the decline in the country’s inflation rate, leaving households under continued pressure from rising housing costs. He explained that lower inflation does not necessarily mean rental prices will fall. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on August 25, he said that the decline in inflation only indicates that prices are increasing at a slower rate, while the higher prices established during previous periods of inflation remain in place. “The original two-bedroom rental price hasn’t gone down,” Dr Otoo said. He explained that although the rate of increase in rental prices has slowed, landlords are still charging prices that are significantly higher than previous levels. “In fact, it’s increasing, as we show, at a slower rate,” he added. Dr Otoo said the situation demonstrates the difference between inflation and the actual price level of goods and services. He noted that when inflation falls, consumers may expect the prices of essential items to decline. However, unless there is deflation, prices generally remain at their new, higher levels and may continue to increase, albeit more slowly. The housing market, he said, presents a particular challenge because the shortage of housing units gives landlords greater pricing power. With relatively few housing units available compared with demand, renters often have limited alternatives when faced with high rental charges. Dr Otoo argued that increasing the supply of housing would help create more options for tenants and encourage greater competition in the rental market. He also called for better information on rental prices, saying consumers need reliable information to compare properties and make informed decisions. According to him, greater competition is important because tenants should have the ability to consider alternatives when they believe a particular rental price is too high. The continued pressure on rent prices also highlights the wider challenge of household incomes failing to keep pace with the cost of living. Dr Otoo noted that while inflation has improved, income levels have not necessarily increased at the same rate as prices, leaving many households struggling to absorb the cost of housing and other essential expenses. He therefore stressed that the improvement in inflation figures should not be mistaken for a significant reduction in the cost of living. For many renters, the key concern remains the actual amount they pay each month, rather than simply the rate at which prices are increasing.

items.title: UNIZIK suspends professor stripped over alleged sexual assault
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu The management of Nnamdi Azikiwe University (NAU), Awka, Anambra State, has suspended Professor Ifeanyi Odinye of the Department of Chinese Studies for a period of three months over alleged sexual molestation of a student, which , it said, violated the university’s General and Academic Regulations. The Vice Chancellor of the University, Prof. Ugochukwu Anyaehie approved the suspension of Prof Odinye with half salary in the first instance, following the recommendations of the six- man special investigative panel which submitted its preliminary report on 21st August 2026. The student involved in the unfortunate incident, Chikamso Favour Okechukwu, according to the directive of the Vice Chancellor, has been referred to the student’s examination misconduct committee Odinye was physically assaulted and stripped on 15 August by some angry students over an alleged attempt to sexually molest a female student of the university. A video clip that went viral showed a female student coming out of Odinye’s office with his clothes, claiming that the lecturer attempted to assault her sexually in the office. She was heard shouting that the lecturer had attempted to rape her, while other people believed to be students were seen pursuing the lecturer who boarded a tricycle that drove out of the premises The embattled lecturer wore an academic academic gown at the time of the incident after the student left his office with his dress. The viral video also showed some men hitting the lecturer, who was completely stripped within the university premises, while the female student, who was seen crying after running out of the lecturer’s office. She was said have pretended to agreed for a sexual encounter until the lecturer had removed his clothes, which she ran away with. The Public Relations Officer of the university, Mr. Aloysius Attah said in a statement that the Vice Chancellor has also extended the duration of the committee for another two weeks to enable the team complete its assignment and address in full, the five – point terms of reference. Attah said the panel, chaired by Prof. Emmanuel Obidimma, Provost, College of Postgraduate Studies, in the preliminary report, dealt on two issues out of the five for determination and indicted Prof Odinye for contravening Section 5.8.3 of the General and Academic Regulations (GAR) of Nnamdi Azikiwe University by failing to, not only record and submit the case of examination misconduct against Chikamso Favour Okechukwu on the prescribed examination misconduct Report Form, but also gave back the offending phone recovered during the examination to the student on the same day in total disregard to section 5.8.1(iv) of the GAR. According to him, the other three issues for determination by the committee are to be addressed within the two weeks. The issues to be determined are whether there was sexual harassment, identify the persons involved in the assault meted to Prof. Odinye and whether there was any incident of kidnapping in the matter. “The committee members are expected to conclude their findings with recommendations to the Vice Chancellor before a final verdict is initiated, including possible criminal prosecution”, the PRO said. He added that the Vice Chancellor reiterated the stance of his administration’s prioritization of staff/ student’s welfare and zero tolerance to unethical practices, while upholding the principles of transparency and fair hearing. The post UNIZIK suspends professor stripped over alleged sexual assault appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana’s low-wage structure rooted in colonial labour system — TUC’s Dr Otoo
items.description: Deputy Secretary-General of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), Dr Kwabena Nyarko Otoo, has attributed Ghana’s low salaries and wages to labour practices introduced during the colonial era. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, August 25, Dr Otoo said historical accounts suggested that Ghanaian workers who received comparatively high wages were able to meet their financial targets, save money and leave their jobs within about six months. According to him, the practice created labour shortages despite the availability of jobs, prompting colonial employers to reduce wages to retain workers for longer periods. “The low salary has a historical antecedent, when wage and work were introduced in Ghana. According to the British, the Ghanaian worker has a target mentality: if you pay them well and they hit their target within six months, they stop the work. So, higher pay, according to them, reduced labour supply. So the pay they could give you in six months, they extended it to one year, and that is the genesis, and we have not been able to overcome it,” he disclosed. Dr Otoo said the colonial wage policy compelled employees to remain at work for longer as they struggled to achieve their financial goals, helping employers maintain a stable workforce. He argued that although colonial rule had ended, the low-wage structure it created had remained embedded in Ghana’s labour market, contributing to the persistently low earnings of many workers. Dr Otoo was on the show to discuss the cost of living in the country.

items.title: Zorgho : « Utile Pinceau » initie 15 enfants au dessin et à la peinture
items.description: Burkina/Ganzourgou-Art-Pinceau-Formation-Clôture Zorgho : « Utile Pinceau » initie 15 enfants au dessin et à la peinture Zorgho, 24 août 2026 (AIB) – Quinze enfants âgés de 6 à 17 ans ont pris part, du 18 au 24 août 2026 à Zorgho, à une session de formation au dessin et à la peinture, organisée dans le cadre du projet « Utile Pinceau », à l’initiative de l’enseignant et artiste peintre Augustin Kaboré. La clôture a connu la participation des parents des apprenants. Prévue pour dix enfants, la session a finalement accueilli 15 participants en raison de la demande, selon M. Kaboré. Pendant sept jours, les apprenants ont été initiés aux différentes étapes de la création artistique, du dessin à la peinture. « En somme, il y a trois phases : au niveau du tableau, sur le papier avec les crayons et sur le tableau avec la peinture », a expliqué Augustin Kaboré. Les travaux ont porté sur le thème de l’environnement. Les enfants ont notamment réalisé des paysages de village, des arbres, des canaris, des calebasses, des cases… L’initiative visait aussi à les sensibiliser à la plantation et à la protection des arbres. Pour le promoteur, le dessin constitue un moyen de développer la créativité, la concentration et la capacité à imaginer et à réaliser des objets. Il estime que ces apprentissages peuvent également servir dans d’autres métiers, notamment la menuiserie, la maçonnerie et la soudure. Le projet « Utile Pinceau » a été lancé en 2019. La session de 2026 constitue sa quatrième édition. Selon Augustin Kaboré, l’initiative fait face à plusieurs difficultés, dont l’insuffisance de matériel et de professionnels pour encadrer les enfants, ainsi que le manque d’un espace adapté. La disponibilité des parents pour accompagner les enfants et le choix de la période des vacances figurent également parmi les contraintes. Le parent d’apprenant Charles Auguste Korsaga a salué les acquis de la session. Il a indiqué que ses trois enfants participants ont développé leur concentration et leur intérêt pour le dessin. Il a invité d’autres parents à inscrire leurs enfants au projet. De son côté, le parent d’apprenant Saïdou Bandé a relevé des changements chez son enfant, notamment dans l’expression orale et la reproduction à domicile des exercices appris pendant les séances. Le promoteur a invité les parents à accompagner leurs enfants dans la pratique artistique. Pour lui, l’objectif n’est pas nécessairement d’en faire des peintres, mais de développer leurs capacités à travailler avec leurs mains et leur imagination. La cérémonie de clôture a été marquée par la présentation des œuvres réalisées par les apprenants aux parents. Pour les sessions de vacances, « Utile Pinceau » accueille les enfants âgés de 6 à 17 ans. Des sessions destinées aux adultes sont également organisées. Agence d’information du Burkina MS-DNK

items.title: Gaoua | Prix des produits de grande consommation : La BMCRF ferme certains commerces
items.description: La direction régionale du commerce a mené une opération coup de poing le lundi 24 août 2026 à Gaoua, en collaboration avec la Police nationale. Les inspections ont révélé de multiples infractions, de l’absence d’affichage à la vente de produits prohibés, entraînant des sanctions immédiates. Hier, les agents de la DRICA-Djôrô, épaulés par les forces de l’ordre, ont arpenté les artères commerçantes de Gaoua dans le cadre d’un contrôle intensif des prix et de la qualité des produits. Cette descente terrain visait à vérifier la conformité des étiquetages et la loyauté des pratiques commerciales auprès des détaillants. Les manquements relevés par les inspecteurs sont significatifs. Outre l’absence fréquente d’affichage des prix, qui empêche le consommateur de connaître le tarif réel, certaines enseignes ont été épinglées pour publicité mensongère. Plus grave, la vente de farine de blé, dont l’importation est formellement interdite, a été constatée sur plusieurs étals. Face à ces infractions, les autorités n’ont pas usé de demi-mesures. Des lots de marchandises ont été saisis et retirés de la vente, tandis que des boutiques ont été placées sous scellés. Les gérants contrevenants ont été convoqués pour s’expliquer sur leurs agissements et devront répondre de leurs actes devant les instances compétentes. À l’issue de cette opération, le Directeur régional a tenu à rappeler les règles en vigueur, insistant sur la nécessité pour les commerçants de garantir une transparence totale afin de protéger le pouvoir d’achat des populations. Il a également profité de cette sortie pour réitérer les tarifs officiels du gaz domestique applicables à Gaoua, fixés à 2 240 FCFA pour la bonbonne de 6 kilogrammes et à 6 000 FCFA pour celle de 12 kilogrammes, invitant les consommateurs à la vigilance. Minute.bf

items.title: Comoé : Un nouveau Conseil d’administration installé à la tête de la SOSUCO pour relever les défis de l’entreprise
items.description: Burkina-Tannounyan-Comoé-Banfora-SOSUCO-Installation-Nouveau-PCA-Membres Comoé : Un nouveau Conseil d’administration installé à la tête de la SOSUCO pour relever les défis de l’entreprise Banfora, 23 août 2026, (AIB) – Le secrétaire général du ministère de l’Industrie, du commerce et de l’artisanat a présidé, le jeudi 20 août 2026 au nom du ministre, l’installation officielle du nouveau président du Conseil d’administration (PCA) de la Société sucrière de la Comoé (SOSUCO) et des membres du Conseil d’administration. Au total, sept membres composent ce nouveau Conseil, y compris le PCA. La cérémonie d’installation du nouveau Conseil d’administration de la SOSUCO marque une nouvelle étape dans la vie de cette entreprise stratégique du Burkina Faso. Présidant la cérémonie au nom du ministre de l’Industrie, du commerce et de l’artisanat, le secrétaire général du ministère a adressé ses félicitations au nouveau président du Conseil d’administration ainsi qu’à l’ensemble des administrateurs. Dans son intervention, il les a exhortés à assumer pleinement les responsabilités qui leur sont confiées et à accomplir leur mission avec abnégation, engagement et sens du devoir. Il a également souhaité plein succès au PCA dans l’exercice de ses nouvelles fonctions, ainsi qu’à l’ensemble des membres du Conseil. Le secrétaire général a particulièrement insisté sur la nécessité d’une collaboration étroite entre le Conseil d’administration, la direction générale et l’ensemble des collaborateurs de la SOSUCO. Pour lui, cette synergie est indispensable pour permettre à l’entreprise de relever efficacement les défis auxquels elle est confrontée et d’atteindre les objectifs qui lui sont assignés. Il a ainsi invité les administrateurs à travailler dans un esprit de cohésion, de complémentarité et de responsabilité, afin de contribuer davantage au développement et à la performance de la société. Prenant la parole à son tour, le directeur général, de la SOSUCO, Ouattara Djakaridja Hema s’est réjoui de la nomination du nouveau président et des membres du Conseil d’administration. Il a exprimé sa reconnaissance aux plus hautes autorités du pays pour cette décision, qu’il considère comme un appui important pour l’entreprise. Selon lui, la mise en place de ce nouveau Conseil constitue une opportunité pour renforcer la gouvernance et accompagner davantage la SOSUCO dans la réalisation de ses missions. Il a réaffirmé la disponibilité de la direction générale à travailler en étroite collaboration avec les administrateurs pour faire face aux différents défis de l’entreprise. . Dans son allocution circonstancielle de prise de fonctions, le nouveau président du Conseil d’administration, Hadi Honoré Yonli, a d’abord rendu grâce à Dieu et sollicité sa grâce et sa miséricorde pour la réussite de la mission qui lui est confiée. Il a ensuite exprimé sa profonde gratitude aux plus hautes autorités du Burkina Faso, particulièrement au Ministre, pour la confiance placée en sa personne. Se présentant comme un « humble serviteur de la République », le nouveau PCA a assuré qu’il entendait se montrer digne de cette confiance. Il a également engagé les administrateurs, la direction générale et le personnel de la SOSUCO à œuvrer ensemble pour mener à bien la mission confiée à l’entreprise. Le PCA a par ailleurs annoncé son intention de mobiliser l’ensemble des membres du Conseil et le personnel autour des défis et objectifs qui sont assignés à la société. Il a aussi indiqué qu’il n’hésiterait pas à solliciter, au besoin, les conseils et orientations des autorités de tutelle afin de contribuer à la satisfaction des besoins de la population en sucre. La cérémonie s’est achevée sur une note d’engagement et d’espoir pour l’avenir de la SOSUCO, avec un appel à la mobilisation collective autour des objectifs de l’entreprise et de sa contribution à l’approvisionnement du pays en sucre. A l’issue de la cérémonie d’installation officielle, le nouveau président et l’ensemble des membres du Conseil d’administration de la SOSUCO ont été présenté aux travailleurs de l’entreprise. Cette présentation a permis aux agents de faire connaissance avec les nouveaux responsables appelés à accompagner la direction générale dans la conduite et le développement de la société. Agence d’information du Burkina JPY-DNK

items.title: Fulham vs Chelsea: Joao Pedro makes history as Chelsea’s No.9 curse ends
items.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Joao Pedro made a dream start to life as Chelsea’s new No.9, scoring just 31 seconds into the Blues’ Premier League opener against Fulham on Monday. The Brazilian forward opened the scoring at Craven Cottage with a brilliant chip over Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno after being played through by Cole Palmer. Pedro’s early strike not only gave new Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso the perfect start to his reign but also ended the club’s long-running struggles associated with the No.9 shirt. The shirt has been worn by several high-profile forwards over the years, including Fernando Torres, Radamel Falcao, Alvaro Morata, Gonzalo Higuain, Romelu Lukaku and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang, with many failing to consistently find the net. Liam Delap, who wore the number last season after joining Chelsea from Ipswich for £30m, scored just once in the Premier League while wearing it. He is now reportedly close to a £40m move to Nottingham Forest. Pedro, who recently signed a new eight-year contract with Chelsea, wasted no time in showing he could have a very different relationship with the shirt. His 31-second effort also set a new record for the fastest goal scored on the opening matchday of a Premier League season. Chelsea went on to secure a 3-2 victory, with Morgan Rogers and Palmer also finding the net, while Josh King and Gonzalo Garcia scored for Fulham. For Pedro, however, the night was particularly significant as he appeared to put the infamous Chelsea No.9 curse to rest almost immediately. items.title: Young people must be at the table, not merely spoken about – NYA CEO Osman Ayariga
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the National Youth Authority (NYA), Osman Abdulai Ayariga, has called for greater inclusion of young people in decision-making processes, insisting that the youth must be given a direct voice in shaping policies that affect their lives. Speaking at the National Youth Parliament Mock Sitting, Mr Ayariga said young people had for too long been the subject of discussions on issues such as unemployment, education, skills development, entrepreneurship and governance without being adequately represented in the rooms where decisions were made. He said young people were not “citizens-in-waiting” but active participants in Ghana’s development who already contribute as students, workers, entrepreneurs, professionals, voters and community leaders. He therefore urged institutions to create meaningful opportunities for the youth to participate in governance and national discourse. “Young people must not only be spoken about in rooms where decisions are made. Young people must be present in those rooms,” Mr Ayariga said. He stressed that meaningful participation required more than simply giving young people platforms to speak, arguing that they must also be equipped with the knowledge, competence and confidence to contribute effectively. “Do not come merely because you are young. Come because you have ideas. Come because you have studied the issues,” he said.

items.title: PIB par habitant : la France passe sous la moyenne de l’UE
items.description: Dans les annees 2000, le produit interieur brut par habitant de la France, mesure en standards de pouvoir d'achat, se situait environ a 15 % au-dessus de la moyenne de l'Union europeenne. Depuis 2022, il evolue en dessous. En 2025, l'indice francais atteint 98 (base 100 pour l'UE), soit un niveau comparable a celui de Chypre. Un glissement progressif plutot qu'un effondrement « Nous n'avons plus les memes moyens qu'avant. […] Aujourd'hui, nous sommes passes en dessous de la moyenne. Cela signifie que nous sommes moins riches qu'avant », souligne Mathieu Plane, economiste a l'OFCE. Les chiffres d'Eurostat et de l'Insee confirment ce decrochage relatif : en 2025, le PIB par habitant francais s'etablit autour de 40 700 SPA, contre 41 600 pour la moyenne de l'UE a 27 et 43 300 pour la zone euro. Laure Closier, journaliste economique sur BFM TV evoque des chiffres « mauvais » et « l'Espagne, l'Italie, la Grece, Chypre sont meilleurs que la France » evoquant notamment les efforts faits par ces etats en matiere de deficit public la ou la France continue de voir ses depenses grimper . L’effondrement du PIB/habitant des Français choque toute la presse. "Les Français sont de moins en moins riches. L’Espagne, l’Italie, la Grèce, Chypre sont meilleurs que la France." Le Grand Déclassement est devenu le Grand Appauvrissement. pic.twitter.com/hEntWSzSU2 — Sir 𝕏 (@SirAfuera) August 24, 2026 Ce recul s'explique par une combinaison de facteurs : gains de productivite atones, desindustrialisation, faiblesse relative de l'education (recul dans les classements PISA) et dette publique elevee, qui limite les marges de manœuvre. La France reste la deuxieme economie de l'UE en volume, mais son avance s'est erodee face au rattrapage de certains pays d'Europe de l'Est et a la performance de voisins comme l'Allemagne ou les Pays-Bas. En janvier deja, l'Insee, veritable reference francaise confirmait : « En 2024, le produit interieur brut (PIB) par habitant de la France, exprime en standards de pouvoir d'achat, est inferieur de 1 % a la moyenne de l'Union europeenne a 27 pays ». Bonjour et merci de mobiliser nos données dans le cadre du débat public. En 2024, le produit intérieur brut (PIB) par habitant de la France, exprimé en standards de pouvoir d'achat, est inférieur de 1 % à la moyenne de l’Union européenne à 27 pays. 👉 https://t.co/ixNASjKPpr — Insee (@InseeFr) January 29, 2026 Des economistes parlent d'un « lent declin » plutot que d'un decrochage brutal. Le PIB par habitant ne mesure pas seul le niveau de vie : la consommation et les prestations sociales pesent lourd en France, mais il reste un indicateur clef de la richesse produite.

items.title: Automobile, tourisme, commerce : 22,757 milliards d’euros d’échanges entre le Maroc et l’Espagne en 2025
items.description: Les relations économiques entre le Maroc et l’Espagne continuent de gagner en intensité. En 2025, les échanges commerciaux entre les deux pays ont atteint 22,757 milliards d’euros, illustrant la profondeur d’un partenariat qui s’étend bien au-delà du commerce de marchandises pour englober l’industrie, l’investissement et le tourisme. Cette dynamique repose notamment sur la complémentarité des deux économies et sur leur proximité géographique, un atout qui favorise l’intégration croissante des chaînes de production, en particulier dans les secteurs de l’automobile et du textile. Selon les données relayées par l’agence espagnole EFE à partir du rapport-pays de l’ ICEX , l’Union européenne demeure le principal partenaire commercial du Royaume. En 2024, elle a représenté la première source d’approvisionnement du Maroc, avec des exportations vers le Royaume évaluées à 34,148 milliards d’euros, tout en constituant son premier débouché commercial avec 26,958 milliards d’euros d’importations marocaines. Au sein de l’Union européenne, l’Espagne conserve sa place de premier partenaire commercial du Maroc, aussi bien pour les exportations que pour les importations. Une croissance qui se poursuit en 2026 Les données du premier semestre 2026 confirment la poursuite de cette dynamique. Les exportations espagnoles vers le Maroc ont progressé de 3,5 % pour atteindre 6,4205 milliards d’euros, soit 3,2 % de l’ensemble des ventes espagnoles à l’étranger. Dans le même temps, les importations espagnoles en provenance du Maroc ont augmenté de 4,1 %, à 5,7955 milliards d’euros, représentant 2,5 % du total des achats extérieurs de l’Espagne. Cette évolution s’inscrit dans une tendance de long terme. Après une progression particulièrement soutenue des échanges bilatéraux en 2017 (+12,8 %), le rythme de croissance s’est modéré à partir de 2018, restant inférieur à 3 % par an. L’année 2025 a néanmoins été marquée par un recul de 4,1 % des exportations espagnoles vers le Maroc, conséquence notamment de la baisse des ventes de carburants liée à l’augmentation des importations marocaines de diesel russe. À l’inverse, les importations espagnoles de produits marocains ont progressé de 6 %. L’automobile, pilier de l’intégration industrielle L’industrie automobile demeure l’un des principaux moteurs de la coopération économique entre Rabat et Madrid. Premier secteur exportateur du Maroc, elle écoule près de 90 % de sa production sur les marchés internationaux, avec l’Union européenne comme destination privilégiée. L’Espagne absorbe à elle seule environ 20 % des exportations marocaines du secteur automobile, témoignant du degré d’interconnexion entre les deux économies. Le développement de cette filière s’accompagne d’un renforcement de la présence des fournisseurs espagnols au Maroc. L’ICEX souligne notamment le rôle du cluster industriel du Pays basque, qui regroupe plus de 90 entreprises fournissant au secteur automobile marocain des matériaux et composants à forte valeur ajoutée, dont l’acier vert. Pour Manuel Antonio Fernández-Villacañas, professeur à l’école de commerce EAE, la proximité géographique constitue un avantage stratégique majeur. Dans un secteur où les chaînes logistiques jouent un rôle déterminant, la courte distance entre les deux pays demeure un facteur de compétitivité difficilement substituable. Le tourisme, autre vecteur de rapprochement Le tourisme figure également parmi les principaux leviers des relations économiques bilatérales. Selon les données du ministère marocain du Tourisme citées par EFE, le Royaume a accueilli en 2025 près de 4,6 millions de visiteurs espagnols, soit une hausse de 12 % par rapport à l’année précédente. L’Espagne se classe ainsi au deuxième rang des marchés émetteurs de touristes vers le Maroc, derrière la France. Cette progression confirme l’importance croissante des flux touristiques dans le renforcement des liens économiques entre les deux pays, au moment où le Royaume poursuit sa stratégie de développement de l’industrie touristique et de diversification de ses partenariats internationaux. items.title: Denmark, UK, France back US proposal to expand Sudan arms embargo – China, Russia oppose
items.description: A US proposal to expand the arms embargo on Darfur to cover drones and the whole of Sudan has prompted widespread reactions among representatives of countries taking part in Monday’s UN Security Council session on Sudan. Representatives of Denmark, Britain, and France backed the US proposal, while China, Russia, and Sudan’s UN representative opposed it. Sudan’s army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, Abdelfattah El Burhan, meanwhile, played down the potential impact of any additional sanctions or embargo on the country in a speech at a police graduation ceremony in Khartoum. As reported previously by Radio Dabanga, the USA has proposed expanding the arms embargo currently imposed on Sudan’s Darfur region to cover the entire country, in an attempt to stem the flow of weapons and drones fuelling the war that has continued since April 2023. Massad Boulos, the US president’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, told the UN Security Council session on Sudan on Monday that more than 12 countries were providing various forms of military support to the two warring parties, helping to prolong the conflict and increase civilian casualties. The US proposals include clarifying that the arms embargo covers drones, their components, and related technologies, as well as strengthening the capacity of the panel of experts responsible for monitoring sanctions and increasing its cooperation with other UN sanctions teams and panels. Call to extend ICC jurisdiction to all of Sudan Denmark’s foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, whose country holds the Security Council presidency for August, also called for the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court to be extended to cover the whole of Sudan. Speaking to the session, Rasmussen said the Security Council had a responsibility to stop the war, which he said was destabilising the entire region. He called for a humanitarian truce leading to a ceasefire, describing it as “the only way to achieve genuine protection for civilians”. Russia’s representative to the Security Council, Vasily A Nebenzya, said his country opposed the US proposal to expand Security Council sanctions or the arms embargo on Sudan. “Recently, we have heard worrying assessments of the expanding use of combat drones in the context of the Sudanese conflict, amid calls for a comprehensive ban on supplying the country with these systems and related technologies,” Nebenzya told the council. “We agree that attack drones pose a serious threat.” Nebenzya said the Rapid Support Forces did not use drones merely in a random and indiscriminate manner, but often deployed them with the aim of causing the greatest possible damage to civilian infrastructure and civilian populations. By contrast, he said, the Sudanese Armed Forces sought to be precise when carrying out attacks. “It is unacceptable to claim that both sides of the conflict bear equal responsibility for the consequences of weapons use,” he said, arguing that one side was spreading chaos and violence, while the other was essentially conducting an operation to neutralise those who were, in reality, rebels destroying the country. ‘Sanctions are borne by Sudanese citizens’ The Russian representative also expressed dissatisfaction with sanctions imposed on Sudan, pointing to an EU ban on imports of Sudanese gold imposed last July. He said Washington had also expanded its restrictions, including a ban on international financial institutions providing credit, or financial and technical assistance, to Sudan. “We consider such measures unacceptable and hostile towards the country’s government,” he said. “At a time when the Sudanese economy is suffering from years of conflict, and the state needs resources more than ever to rehabilitate the health sector, water supplies, agriculture, and other essential infrastructure, this policy of economic strangulation raises serious questions.” He stressed that ordinary Sudanese would ultimately bear the greatest burden of the consequences of the new restrictions. “From the same perspective, we view any attempts to expand the existing UN Security Council sanctions regime against Sudan,” he said. “We are convinced that the way to alleviate the suffering of the Sudanese people does not lie in continuing to drain the Sudanese economy, but in ending hostilities, expanding humanitarian assistance, and supporting the country’s recovery efforts.” China opposes external solutions China’s representative praised steps taken by Sudan’s government to facilitate humanitarian operations, saying that sanctions were a means rather than an end in themselves. He stressed that the Security Council should respect Sudan’s sovereignty and institutions, adding that China did not support imposing external solutions on the country. Khartoum rejects expansion Sudan’s representative to the UN, El Harith Idris, rejected the expansion of the arms embargo beyond its current scope during the Security Council deliberations. He said the draft resolution would effectively equate the army with the Rapid Support Forces and undermine Sudan’s sovereignty. Idris called on the Security Council instead to renew the existing measures while strengthening their enforcement against those violating the arms embargo, and to subject external networks supplying weapons and drones to greater scrutiny. He said the government was committed to protecting its citizens to the greatest extent possible, having established a national mechanism for civilian protection and worked to facilitate the return of displaced people. By the end of June, he said, 5.8 million voluntary returns had been recorded. Idris said the government remained committed to international humanitarian law and international human rights law, and that security forces were redeploying as control over territory was restored. ‘The people will not break’ In Khartoum, army chief and Sovereignty Council head Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan said talk of possible sanctions against the country would have no effect and would not weaken Sudan’s resolve. Speaking on Monday at a graduation ceremony for the 22nd intake of police officers at the Police Sciences and Law College in Khartoum, El Burhan said: “Our lives and our destiny are in God’s hands.” He urged Sudanese not to pay attention to what he described as claims by “enemies and those with ulterior motives” about the imposition of a no-fly zone over the country. “Our message to those staying in hotels abroad and applauding sanctions to subjugate the Sudanese people is that the people will not break, and collapse and disappointment will befall you,” he said. He added that those people would not be able to rule the Sudanese people again.
